# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Please check yours.

Moose was still damp when I got him out of the van.

He’s a Bernese, and we were halfway through drying him when I smelled hot plastic. He was delighted by the unexpected change of plans. Side door open, back outside, his mum right there. Excellent afternoon, as far as Moose was concerned.

I was shaking.

Everyone is okay. I want to say that first. Moose is okay, I’m okay, and this didn’t turn into the fire it could have been. But the cable supplying my inverter melted at a connection while I was working, and my van is now off the road for at least three weeks.

So far, I’ve cancelled 31 appointments. The repair quote is $4,200. My insurance answer is currently “maybe,” with an adjuster due Thursday. Rent is still due on the first, because apparently rent does not care what your inverter is doing.

I’m writing this partly because I need to get it out of my head, and partly because another groomer I know is about to pay a deposit to the same builder.

Tasha, please read this before you send that money.

And to the other groomers reading: I’m not an electrician. This is what happened in my van, what the electrician who inspected it explained to me, and what I wish I’d asked before I trusted a tidy-looking installation with my dog clients and my whole income.

## What happened in the driveway

On Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 p.m., I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford, drying Moose with the dryer on high.

The first warning was the smell. Hot plastic. I initially thought it was the dryer motor, because that was the thing running right in front of me.

Then I saw smoke coming from the bench seat where the batteries are.

I shut off the battery switch and got Moose out through the side door. I also used the extinguisher a little. I honestly don’t know whether that was necessary, and I’m not going to rewrite the story to make myself sound calm and competent about every second of it.

The positive cable connection was blackened. The insulation had melted back roughly three centimetres.

Moose’s mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. I keep thinking about that part. You can be having a completely normal workday, worrying about your next appointment, and then suddenly you’re sitting outside someone’s house trying to hold a coffee steady.

If you ever smell burning or see smoke in your own van, please don’t stay inside trying to find the exact fault. Get people and animals out, stay clear, and call 911 for smoke or a suspected fire. Only operate an accessible shutoff if you can do it without putting yourself in danger. Don’t go back into smoke to reach it.

What I did is an account of what happened, not an emergency procedure to copy.

## What was installed

My van was built by Coastline Van Fitouts, run by Darren, in spring 2025.

The electrical setup includes:

- A 3,000-watt inverter.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.
- A battery-to-inverter cable marked 4 AWG.
- A 300-amp ANL fuse, mounted about 90 centimetres from the battery.

After the incident, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric inspected it.

Her findings included an undersized inverter supply cable for this installation, a poor crimp on the positive cable lug, and a battery fuse located too far from the battery. Her recommendation for the main inverter cable was 2/0 AWG, along with other repairs.

As of writing, Darren hasn’t replied to three texts and an email.

I’m naming the builder because other groomers are making decisions about their vans, and this is relevant information. But I can describe only my own installation, what happened to it, and what Priya found. I haven’t inspected anyone else’s build, and I don’t yet have a response from Darren to include.

## The bit about watts and amps that I wish I’d understood

I used to look at “3,000W inverter” and “roughly 2,000W dryer” and think: fine. The dryer is under the inverter’s rating.

That comparison leaves out a very important bit: how the power gets from the batteries to the inverter.

The inverter turns the batteries’ low-voltage DC power into AC power for appliances. On the 12-volt side, supplying a powerful dryer means carrying a lot of current.

The basic calculation is:

**Amps = watts ÷ volts.**

So, before accounting for losses:

- An 1,800W load at 12V means 150 amps.
- A 2,000W load at 12V means about 167 amps.
- A 3,000W load at 12V means 250 amps.

But an inverter isn’t perfectly efficient. It takes a bit more power from the batteries than it delivers to the appliance.

Using **90% efficiency as an example**, rather than a measured figure for my inverter, those numbers become approximately:

- **167 amps** for an 1,800W load.
- **185 amps** for a 2,000W load.
- **278 amps** for a 3,000W load.

Actual current changes with battery voltage, inverter efficiency and whatever is running at the time. Those are illustrations, not measurements from the incident.

My dryer is roughly an 1,800–2,000W load. The water heater sometimes runs too, but I don’t have a confirmed wattage for it in these notes, and I can’t say it was drawing power at that exact moment.

So my original scribble of “150–250 amps” needed some explaining. The dryer alone can mean well over 150 amps on the battery side, and a fully loaded 3,000W inverter can draw more than 250 amps once losses are included.

Also, those 200Ah labels on the batteries describe capacity. They don’t tell me that every cable, connection, switch or fuse attached to them can safely carry whatever I ask for. The batteries’ own discharge limits matter too.

That was my first big lesson: an inverter’s headline wattage does not prove the rest of the installation is suitable.

## The cable size wasn’t a small detail

The battery-to-inverter cable in my van was 4 AWG.

Priya told me that, for this 3,000W, 12V installation, it should have been 2/0 AWG.

If cable sizes mean nothing to you, they meant nothing to me either. The naming is confusing: 2/0, also called “two-aught,” is substantially thicker than 4 AWG.

I’m deliberately not writing “every 3,000W inverter needs exactly this cable.” That would turn advice about my installation into a universal rule, and it isn’t one.

The correct cable depends on the inverter manufacturer’s requirements, the length of the cable run, the insulation and temperature ratings, how it’s routed, and other installation details. Both the positive and negative current paths need to be considered.

Priya’s recommendation is for my van. Your electrician needs to specify yours.

What I do feel comfortable saying is that cable size isn’t something to accept on the basis of “we always use that” or “it’s been fine so far.” Ask for the actual size and the reason it’s appropriate.

I didn’t. I wish I had.

## The connection was a problem too

The positive cable lug is the metal terminal fitted onto the cable end.

Priya found that the crimp on mine was poor. My very non-technical description in my notes was that it looked as though it had been done with pliers or a hammer instead of the proper crimping equipment.

I don’t know what tool was actually used. What I can say is that Priya identified an inadequate crimp, and heat-shrink tubing had covered it.

From the outside, it had looked finished.

A bad connection can create resistance, and resistance produces heat when current flows through it. At the currents involved here, a small amount of extra resistance can make a serious hot spot.

For scale, **200 amps passing through a connection with just 0.001 ohm of resistance produces 40 watts of heat at that connection**. That isn’t a measurement of my damaged lug. It’s an example of why a tiny resistance can matter so much.

I can’t separate out exactly how much of the damage came from the cable size and how much came from the connection. That’s for the professionals assessing it.

But both matter. A thicker cable doesn’t make a bad crimp acceptable, and a good crimp doesn’t make an undersized cable suitable.

The heat-shrink is the detail that bothers me most. Not because heat-shrink is bad—it has a proper purpose—but because I’d mistaken a neat finish for evidence that the work underneath was right.

Tidy is not the same as right.

## “But didn’t you have a fuse?”

Yes. A 300A ANL fuse.

I had apparently filed “has a fuse” in my brain under “electrical safety handled.”

A fuse is not a temperature alarm for every connection. A poor connection can get dangerously hot while the current remains below the level needed to make the fuse open. Fuses also have time-current characteristics; they don’t necessarily disconnect the instant their labelled current is exceeded.

That means the presence of a 300A fuse doesn’t rule out damaging heat at a cable lug.

The fuse also has to be coordinated with the cable and the equipment. A large fuse is not automatically a better or safer fuse.

Then there was its location.

Mine was approximately 90 centimetres from the battery. Priya said it should be much closer—around 18 centimetres in the arrangement she was discussing.

The reason is that the cable between the battery and that fuse isn’t protected by that fuse against a short to the negative return path. More cable before the fuse means more cable exposed to that particular risk.

Please don’t take my “18 centimetres-ish” note as a universal Canadian van-wiring rule. Exact requirements, measurement methods and permitted exceptions depend on the applicable standard and installation. Have a qualified person identify what applies to yours.

The repair quote includes a Class T fuse. One reason fuse selection matters with lithium batteries is that a fault can involve very high current. A fuse needs an adequate **interrupt rating**—the ability to safely break that fault current—as well as the correct amp rating and DC voltage rating.

That’s not a shopping recommendation from me to buy a Class T fuse and swap it in yourself. The fuse, holder, cables, batteries and inverter need to be assessed together.

## The photos that made it sink in

Priya pulled up my damage photos alongside thermal-camera images of her own van running a similar kind of load.

My connection was blackened, with the insulation melted back. Hers showed very little warming under the conditions she was demonstrating.

It wasn’t a controlled comparison between identical systems, and a thermal image alone can’t certify an installation. Still, seeing those pictures side by side made the explanation much easier to understand.

“Lots of electricity means things get hot” is not a good enough explanation for a connection melting.

I’ve since bought a $40 infrared thermometer from Canadian Tire. I think it can be a useful extra tool, **if someone qualified shows you where and how to use it safely**.

It is not an electrical inspection in a little plastic gun.

Infrared thermometers read surface temperatures. Shiny metal can give misleading readings, covered connections can hide heat, and one cool reading doesn’t prove a system is safe. There isn’t one magic temperature I can give you that means every van is fine.

Please don’t open battery compartments, remove covers or deliberately run a heavy load to investigate a suspected fault yourself. Ask your electrician whether there are safe, accessible monitoring points and what changes should prompt you to stop using the system.

Mine is not getting switched back on so I can see how hot it gets.

## A power-off checklist for the rest of us

This is a **look-and-document checklist**, not a DIY electrical inspection or repair guide.

And “power off” needs a warning of its own: turning off the inverter or battery switch may not isolate everything. Shore power, solar, vehicle charging and the batteries themselves can still leave parts live.

Follow the shutdown instructions for your installation. If you don’t have them, ask a qualified electrician to provide them. Don’t disconnect battery terminals or improvise an isolation procedure.

With equipment shut down according to those instructions, here’s what we can reasonably check **without removing electrical covers or touching wiring**:

### 1. Look for visible damage

From safely accessible areas, look for melted or discoloured insulation, scorch marks, damaged covers or anything that has visibly changed.

A lingering burnt-plastic smell matters too.

If you find evidence of overheating, leave the system out of use and get professional help. Don’t switch it on “just for a second” to confirm.

### 2. Look at visible cable routing

Can you see cable rubbing against a sharp metal edge? Is something being crushed by stored equipment or a seat? Has loose kit shifted into the electrical area?

Document it without reaching in or moving electrical parts. Don’t pull on a cable to check whether it’s secure.

### 3. Read accessible labels

If you can see them without removing covers, photograph the inverter model, battery labels, cable markings and fuse information.

If you can’t see them safely, put them on the electrician’s list.

“Big red wire” is not a cable specification. That is advice to my past self.

### 4. Check what information you actually have

Do you have a wiring diagram? A component list? Written shutdown instructions? The permitted combinations of appliances you can run?

I want all of that with the repaired van, in terms I understand.

### 5. Check ventilation and storage

Are designated ventilation openings clear? Are towels, bottles or other grooming supplies crowding the electrical equipment?

Don’t dismantle anything to investigate. Ask what clearance the installation requires and keep that space for its intended purpose.

### 6. Check alarms

I had no smoke detector in the back. Just the one in the cab that came with the van.

I’m getting advice on a suitable alarm and placement for the grooming area, including the humidity and temperature conditions it needs to tolerate. Check existing alarms using their test buttons and manufacturer instructions.

I don’t want to assume a cab alarm gives enough warning for a problem under a rear bench.

### 7. Check the extinguisher and exits

Is the extinguisher accessible, secured and within its service requirements? Do you know how to use it? Can you get a dog out without moving a pile of equipment first?

An extinguisher is not a reason to remain inside a smoking van.

### 8. Book the inspection

This is the important bit.

You cannot judge a hidden crimp by looking at heat-shrink. You cannot confirm correct terminal torque by giving it a wiggle. Please don’t tighten terminals, cut insulation away, pull fuses or replace parts as part of this checklist.

Find a qualified electrician experienced with high-current battery systems and mobile installations. Ask them to check the cable sizing, terminations, protection, isolation, charging arrangements and the AC side too—not just the visibly damaged bit.

## Before you pay a builder a deposit

Tasha, this is the section I especially want you to keep.

Ask for the electrical specification **in writing before paying a deposit**, including:

- The inverter make and model, and its installation requirements.
- Battery specifications, including permitted discharge current.
- Main positive and negative cable sizes and planned run lengths.
- Fuse type, amp rating, DC voltage rating, interrupt rating and location.
- How cables will be terminated, supported and protected from damage.
- Which appliances can safely run together.
- Who designs, installs and checks the electrical system.
- Which standards apply to the conversion.
- What inspection, test results, wiring diagram and handover instructions you’ll receive.

Ask whether an independent electrician can inspect the installation before handover, while relevant work is still accessible.

You don’t have to become an electrician to ask those questions. You also don’t have to pretend you understand the answers. Take the specification to someone who does.

A nice-looking fitout, good drawers and neat cable coverings are things I can appreciate. They aren’t proof of electrical safety.

## Where things stand now

The quote is $4,200 for rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and Class T protection. Parts are on order, and the current estimate is at least three weeks off the road.

Thirty-one appointments cancelled so far. Insurance still uncertain. An adjuster coming Thursday. No reply yet from Darren.

I’m relieved nobody was hurt, and I’m scared about money. Both are true. This van is my whole income, and being unable to work while looking at a repair bill is making me feel slightly unhinged.

But I’m not going to rush it back into service because I’m panicking about rent.

Thank you to the clients being patient with me. And thank you to Moose’s mum for the coffee and for sitting with me when I really didn’t want to be left alone yet.

Please get your installation checked if you don’t know whether it’s right. Not because my blog can diagnose your van—it absolutely cannot—but because “it looks tidy” was the reassurance I relied on, and it wasn’t enough.

I’ll post again when the van is back, with what was repaired and what the final checks involved.

Hopefully the next Moose update will just be about how much hair one dog can produce.
